title: AI Selloff Is a Speed Adjustment, Not a Bust, iM Securities Says
excerpt: Semiconductor stocks fell 11.4% in the days around the US midterms while hyperscaler shares rose, a split iM Securities says points to slower AI spending growth, not an end to the investment cycle.
body:
• Comparing November 3 and November 6, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 11.4% while a hyperscaler stock index rose 0.5%, according to iM Securities figures reported by BigGo Finance.
  • iM Securities researcher Park Sang-hyun says AI investment fears after the Democrats' midterm sweep are exaggerated, and that hyperscaler capital spending is unlikely to halt or fall sharply.
  • Data centre construction accounts for only about 11% of total hyperscaler capital expenditure, which limits how far tighter local regulation can cut overall spending.
  • For investors: the firm frames this as spending growth slowing from earlier expectations, not the AI investment boom ending — a distinction that matters before selling chip holdings into the drop.

The fear that swept through semiconductor stocks after the US midterm elections is, on one South Korean brokerage's reading, a repricing of speed rather than a verdict on artificial intelligence itself. In a report dated the 9th, iM Securities researcher Park Sang-hyun argued that the so-called Blue Wave brought AI investment fears to the surface, but that the shock has not spread across the board.

"The Blue Wave brought AI investment fears to the fore, but the shock is not spreading across the board."

— Park Sang-hyun, iM Securities, via BigGo Finance

A selloff with a clear boundary

The price action drew the line. Comparing November 3 and November 6, around the midterms, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.0%, the S&P 500 fell 2.5% and the Nasdaq fell 3.1%. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index plunged 11.4%, and the markets most tied to the chip supply chain fell with it: South Korea's KOSPI dropped 10.4%, Japan's Nikkei 225 dropped 9.0% and Taiwan's Weighted Index dropped 8.3%. The hyperscaler index — the large technology companies actually writing the AI cheques — rose 0.5% over the same comparison.

That divergence is the core of Park's argument. If investors believed AI spending itself was ending, the buyers of the equipment would be falling alongside the sellers. Instead, the impact was concentrated on semiconductor companies and on semiconductor value-chain countries such as South Korea, Japan and Taiwan, rather than on the hyperscalers leading the AI cycle.

What could actually slow

Park does not dismiss the regulatory risk. Tighter scrutiny of data centres after the election could produce construction delays or some scale-backs out of concern for local public opinion. What he disputes is the leap from local permitting friction to a collapse in spending: the market had expected data centre spending to grow in a range from the low teens to about 30% in 2027, and total hyperscaler capital expenditure to rise about 40% to $1 trillion. A slower growth rate against those expectations is a very different event from a halt.

The arithmetic also caps the damage. Data centre construction costs account for only about 11% of total hyperscaler capital expenditure, so even a real slowdown in building touches a minority share of the spending the chip industry ultimately supplies.

A second house reaches a similar conclusion

UBS, in its daily house view, described the same decline as uncertainty about the cost and pace of the data centre buildout rather than a sudden deterioration in the outlook, and as a de-risking event rather than a material change in fundamentals. UBS said proposed US capacity of around 400 gigawatts already far exceeds its buildout assumption of roughly 90 gigawatts by 2030, so regulation is more likely to redistribute and extend the investment cycle than derail it.

What to watch next

Park named three gauges for whether the fear is subsiding: hyperscaler credit default swap premiums, Anthropic's listing, and South Korean semiconductor export trends. Until those indicators point to weakening AI revenue or cloud use, both houses are treating the episode the same way — as the market charging more for the pace of the buildout, not cancelling it.
